Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is a common fungal disease caused by Venturia inaequalis, affecting leaves and fruit, particularly in cool, wet spring weather.
symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots on leaves
causes: Fungal spores (Venturia inaequalis) overwintering in fallen leaves
treatment: Apply fungicides (captan, myclobutanil) starting at bud break
Remove and destroy fallen leaves in autumn
Prune to improve air circulation
Use resistant apple varieties where possible
prevention: Rake and dispose of fallen leaves each autumn
Apply preventive fungicide sprays in early spring

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot is caused by the fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa, affecting leaves, fruit, and bark, and can cause significant fruit loss.
symptoms: Purple spots on leaves that enlarge with concentric rings ('frogeye leaf spot')
Rotting brown to black fruit with concentric rings
causes: Fungal infection from dead wood or mummified fruit
Wounds from insects, hail, or pruning
treatment: Remove and destroy mummified fruit and dead branches
Apply fungicide sprays during the growing season
Prune out cankers well below infected tissue
Sanitize pruning tools between cuts
prevention: Remove mummified fruit and dead wood promptly
Prune out cankers during dormant season
Maintain tree vigor with proper fertilization

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar apple rust is a fungal disease (Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae) that requires both apple/crabapple and cedar/juniper hosts to complete its life cycle.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on upper leaf surface
Orange, gelatinous spore horns on undersides of leaves
Premature leaf drop in severe cases
causes: Fungal spores traveling from nearby juniper/cedar trees
Wet spring weather favoring spore release
treatment: Apply fungicides (myclobutanil, propiconazole) in early spring
Remove nearby juniper/cedar hosts if feasible
Use resistant apple varieties
prevention: Remove galls from nearby juniper trees
Maintain distance between apple trees and junipers
Apply preventive fungicide before infection period

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew is a fungal disease (Podosphaera clandestina) that produces a white, powdery growth on leaves and shoots.
symptoms: White powdery coating on leaves and shoots
causes: Fungal spores favored by warm days and cool nights
High humidity with poor air circulation
treatment: Apply sulfur-based or systemic fungicides
Prune to increase air circulation
Remove heavily infected shoots
prevention: Prune trees to open up canopy

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: Gray leaf spot is caused by the fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis, a major yield-limiting disease of corn in humid regions.
symptoms: Small, rectangular tan to gray lesions bound by leaf veins
Lesions coalesce to blight large areas of leaf
causes: Fungal spores surviving in crop residue
Warm, humid weather with extended leaf wetness
treatment: Apply foliar fungicides at early disease onset
Rotate crops away from corn for 1-2 years
Use resistant hybrids
prevention: Till under crop residue after harvest
Avoid dense planting to improve airflow

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Common rust is caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi, producing reddish-brown pustules on corn leaves.
symptoms: Small, oval, cinnamon-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture releasing powdery rust spores
Leaves may yellow and die in severe infections
treatment: Apply fungicides if infection is severe before tasseling
Use resistant hybrids
Monitor fields regularly during humid weather
prevention: Avoid late planting in high-risk areas
Scout fields early in the season
Apply preventive fungicide in high-risk conditions

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern leaf blight is caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum, producing long, cigar-shaped lesions on corn leaves.
symptoms: Long, elliptical gray-green to tan lesions
Lesions can span several inches along leaf
Lower leaves infected first, spreading upward
Significant leaf blighting in severe cases
causes: Fungal spores surviving in infected crop residue
treatment: Apply foliar fungicides at first sign of disease
Rotate crops with non-host species
Use resistant hybrids

Grape___Black_rot.description: Black rot is a fungal disease caused by Guignardia bidwellii, one of the most destructive diseases of grapes in humid climates.
symptoms: Small tan spots with dark borders on leaves
Reddish-brown lesions on shoots and tendrils
causes: Fungal spores overwintering in mummified fruit and canes
Warm, wet weather during spring and summer
treatment: Apply fungicides from bud break through veraison
Remove and destroy mummified fruit
Prune out infected canes
prevention: Remove mummified berries and infected canes during dormant pruning
Improve canopy airflow through proper training
Apply protective fungicide sprays on a schedule

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: Esca, or Black Measles, is a complex fungal trunk disease affecting grapevines, caused by several wood-rotting fungi.
symptoms: Tiger-stripe pattern of yellow/red discoloration between leaf veins
Sudden vine collapse (apoplexy) in severe cases
causes: Older, stressed vines are more susceptible
treatment: Remove and destroy severely infected vines
Apply wound protectants after pruning
Practice remedial pruning to remove diseased wood
prevention: Prune during dry weather to reduce infection risk
Remove and destroy severely diseased vines promptly

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: Isariopsis leaf spot, or leaf blight, is caused by the fungus Pseudocercospora vitis, affecting grape foliage.
symptoms: Irregular reddish-brown to dark brown spots on leaves
Spots may merge causing large blighted areas
causes: Fungal spores spread by wind and rain
treatment: Apply fungicides at early disease onset
Improve canopy management for airflow
Remove heavily infected leaves

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: Huanglongbing (HLB), or citrus greening, is a devastating bacterial disease spread by the Asian citrus psyllid, with no known cure.
symptoms: Blotchy, asymmetrical yellow mottling on leaves
Small, lopsided, bitter fruit that stays green
causes: Bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter spread by Asian citrus psyllid
Infected nursery stock or grafting material
Psyllid vector presence in the region
treatment: No cure available - remove and destroy infected trees to prevent spread
Control psyllid vector with insecticides
Use certified disease-free nursery stock
prevention: Monitor and remove infected trees promptly
Report suspected cases to agricultural authorities

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni, affecting leaves, fruit, and twigs of peach trees.
symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn purple-brown
causes: Bacteria spread by rain splash and wind
Entry through wounds or natural openings
treatment: Apply copper-based bactericides during dormant season
Prune out infected twigs
Avoid overhead irrigation
prevention: Apply copper sprays preventively in early spring
Avoid working in wet orchards to reduce spread

symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves turning dark brown
causes: Bacteria spread by splashing water and contaminated seed
Working in wet fields spreading bacteria
treatment: Apply copper-based bactericides
Remove and destroy infected plants
Rotate crops away from peppers/tomatoes
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants
Rotate crops for at least 2 years
Avoid working with plants when wet

Potato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is caused by the fungus Alternaria solani, commonly affecting older potato leaves first.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric 'target' rings
causes: Fungal spores surviving in soil and plant debris
Warm temperatures with alternating wet/dry periods
treatment: Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) at first sign of disease
Remove and destroy infected foliage
Ensure adequate plant nutrition, especially nitrogen
prevention: Practice crop rotation (avoid potatoes/tomatoes for 2+ years)

Potato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans, the pathogen responsible for the Irish Potato Famine, and can destroy crops rapidly.
symptoms: Water-soaked, dark green to black lesions on leaves
White fuzzy mold on leaf undersides in humid conditions
Rapid blackening and collapse of foliage
causes: Oomycete spores spread rapidly by wind and rain
Cool, wet weather (60-70°F with high humidity)
Infected seed tubers or volunteer plants
treatment: Apply fungicides preventively (chlorothalonil, copper-based) especially before rain
Destroy infected plants immediately
Harvest tubers only in dry conditions
prevention: Destroy volunteer potato plants and cull piles
Apply protective fungicides during high-risk weather
Ensure good field drainage and airflow

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew is a common fungal disease of squash caused by Podosphaera xanthii and Erysiphe cichoracearum.
symptoms: White, powdery spots on leaves and stems
Spots enlarge and cover entire leaf surface
Yellowing and browning of infected leaves
causes: Warm days and cool, humid nights
treatment: Apply sulfur or potassium bicarbonate-based fungicides
Remove heavily infected leaves
Improve air circulation between plants
prevention: Water at the base to keep foliage dry
Apply preventive fungicide in high-risk seasons

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: Leaf scorch is caused by the fungus Diplocarpon earlianum, causing a scorched appearance on strawberry leaves.
symptoms: Small purple spots on upper leaf surface
Spots merge, giving leaves a scorched, dried appearance
causes: Fungal spores spread by rain splash
Wet foliage from rain or overhead irrigation
treatment: Apply fungicides at first sign of infection
Remove and destroy infected leaves after harvest
Avoid overhead watering
prevention: Renovate beds after harvest (remove old foliage)
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead
Space plants for good air circulation

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas species, affecting tomato leaves, stems, and fruit, especially in warm, wet weather.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves turning dark brown/black
causes: Bacteria spread by splashing water, tools, and contaminated seed
Working with wet plants spreading bacteria
treatment: Apply copper-based bactericides
Remove and destroy infected plant debris
Rotate crops away from tomatoes/peppers
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants
Sanitize tools and avoid working wet plants

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is a fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani that commonly affects tomato leaves, stems, and fruit, especially in warm, humid climates.
symptoms: Dark brown concentric 'target' spots on leaves
Stem lesions and fruit rot near stem end
causes: Fungal spores surviving in soil and plant debris
treatment: Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, copper-based) at first symptoms
Remove and destroy infected lower leaves
Stake plants and mulch to reduce soil splash
prevention: Mulch around plants to prevent soil splash
Water at the base, avoiding wet foliage

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans, a highly destructive disease that can devastate tomato crops within days.
symptoms: Water-soaked, dark green to brown lesions on leaves
White fuzzy mold on leaf undersides in humid weather
Rapid blackening and collapse of foliage
Firm, brown, greasy-looking spots on fruit
causes: Oomycete spores spread rapidly by wind and rain
Cool, wet weather with high humidity
Nearby infected potato or tomato plants
treatment: Apply fungicides preventively (chlorothalonil, copper-based)
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately
Avoid working in wet fields
prevention: Monitor and remove volunteer potato/tomato plants

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Leaf mold is caused by the fungus Passalora fulva (formerly Fulvia fulva), primarily affecting tomatoes grown in greenhouses or humid climates.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots on upper leaf surface
Olive-green to grayish-purple velvety mold on leaf undersides
causes: Fungal spores favored by high humidity (>85%)
treatment: Improve ventilation and reduce humidity
Apply fungicides labeled for leaf mold
Remove and destroy infected leaves
prevention: Increase greenhouse ventilation and reduce humidity

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot is caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici, one of the most common tomato foliar diseases.
symptoms: Small, circular spots with dark borders and light gray centers
Tiny black fungal fruiting bodies visible in spot centers
causes: Fungal spores surviving in soil and plant debris
Warm, wet weather with extended leaf wetness
treatment: Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, copper-based) at first sign
Remove and destroy infected lower leaves
Mulch to reduce soil splash
prevention: Stake plants and mulch around base

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) are tiny pests that feed on tomato leaves, causing stippling and, in severe cases, plant decline.
symptoms: Fine webbing on leaf undersides and between leaves
Leaves turn bronze/yellow and dry out
Reduced plant vigor in heavy infestations
causes: Hot, dry weather favoring mite reproduction
treatment: Apply miticides or insecticidal soap
Introduce predatory mites as biological control
Spray plants with water to dislodge mites
prevention: Monitor plants regularly during hot, dry periods

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Target spot is caused by the fungus Corynespora cassiicola, producing target-like lesions on tomato leaves, stems, and fruit.
symptoms: Brown lesions with concentric rings, resembling a target
Lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit
causes: Fungal spores spread by wind and rain
treatment: Apply fungicides at early disease onset
Remove and destroy infected plant debris
Improve air circulation through pruning
prevention: Rotate crops away from tomato for 1-2 years
Stake and prune plants for airflow

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) is transmitted by whiteflies and can cause severe stunting and yield loss.
symptoms: Upward curling and yellowing of leaves
Flower drop and poor fruit set
causes: Virus transmitted by silverleaf/sweetpotato whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
treatment: No cure - remove and destroy infected plants
Control whitefly populations with insecticides or biological control
Use reflective mulches to repel whiteflies
prevention: Control whiteflies with row covers or insecticides

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) is a highly stable, contagious virus that causes mottling and distortion of tomato foliage and fruit.
symptoms: Mottled light and dark green pattern on leaves
Leaf curling, distortion, and fern-like growth
Internal browning or mottling of fruit
causes: Virus spread through contaminated seed, tools, and hands
Mechanical transmission via contact with infected plants
Highly stable virus surviving in plant debris and soil
treatment: No cure - remove and destroy infected plants
Disinfect tools and hands with a bleach or milk solution
Avoid handling plants when wet
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed and resistant varieties
Avoid tobacco use near plants (can carry related virus)
